title: The chronobiology textbook
lede: Twelve chapters on the rhythms of living things, from the molecular clock to migration, written by the students of one class.
description: The class's chronobiology textbook: twelve chapters on circadian, ultradian and infradian rhythms.

figure-1.alt: Cycle diagram of the molecular clock, about 24 hours long: CLOCK and BMAL1 switch on the Per and Cry genes, the PER and CRY proteins build up and block CLOCK-BMAL1, then break down so the cycle restarts.

figure-1-2.alt: Pathway diagram: tryptophan becomes 5-hydroxytryptophan, then serotonin, then N-acetylserotonin, then melatonin, each step made by an enzyme (TPH, 5-HTP decarboxylase, AANAT and HIOMT).

figure-2.alt: Flow diagram: daylight reaches the retina, which signals the SCN in the hypothalamus; the SCN coordinates local clocks in the liver, pancreas, heart and skeletal muscle, which also respond to feeding, hormones and temperature.

figure-2-2.alt: Diagram of a rodent brain: light reaches the SCN from the retina through the retinohypothalamic tract, while serotonin from the raphe nuclei and signals from the IGL and locus coeruleus carry non-light input to the clock.

figure-3.alt: Illustration of a person's head showing the signal path from the eye to the SCN, then down through the spinal cord and neck ganglia to the pineal gland, which makes melatonin in darkness.

figure-1.alt: Graph of pilots' response speed on a vigilance test by flight arrival time: mean speed stays near 4 responses per second at all times, while the slowest 10 percent of responses are about 2.2 to 2.7.

figure-1-2.alt: Illustration of circadian misalignment: a person's silhouette between an external clock at 11 p.m. at night and an internal clock at 7 a.m. in daylight.

subsections: How are hunger and digestion related?

How alcohol affects the metabolism cycle

figure-1.alt: Flow diagram of GLP-1 signaling: food reaches the small intestine, which releases GLP-1; through the blood it triggers insulin secretion in the pancreas, and through the vagus nerve it signals fullness to the brain.

figure-1-2.alt: Venn diagram: melatonin and cortisol belong to the master clock, the food-entrainable oscillator and GLP-1 to peripheral clocks, and insulin, leptin and ghrelin to both.

figure-2.alt: Anatomical drawing of the body labeled with hunger signals: ghrelin made in the stomach, GLP-1 in the ileum, leptin in fat tissue, GLP-1 detected by the pancreas, and the brain responding to these hormones.

figure-4.alt: Diagram showing that while the liver processes ethanol, its usual metabolism of food and drink, mainly glucose, into ATP is blocked.

figure-5.alt: Diagram of aerobic respiration: glycolysis in the cytosol turns glucose into pyruvate, then pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain in the mitochondria produce most of the ATP, with NADH and FADH2 carrying electrons.

figure-6.alt: Reaction diagram: alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into acetaldehyde, then aldehyde dehydrogenase turns it into acetic acid, each step converting NAD+ to NADH.

figure-1.alt: Graph of mean daytime oral temperature from 8:00 to 24:00 for morning, intermediate and evening types; the morning type peaks earlier in the day than the evening type.

outline: Getting a signal from a recording

figure-11.alt: Leaky integrate-and-fire formula: tau m times d V over d t equals minus the quantity V of t minus V rest, plus R m times I of t.

figure-12.alt: Fourier transform formula: X of f equals the integral from minus infinity to infinity of x of t times e to the minus i 2 pi f t, d t.

figure-13.alt: Wavelet transform formula: W of a and b equals 1 over the square root of a, times the integral of x of t times the complex conjugate of psi of t minus b over a, d t.

figure-14.alt: Artificial neuron formula: y equals phi of the sum over i of w i times x i, plus b.

figure-15.alt: Leaky integrate-and-fire formula: tau m times d V over d t equals minus the quantity V of t minus V rest, plus R m times I of t.

figure-23.alt: Handwritten outline notes for section 1, What is being measured: electrodes record voltage, spikes as action potentials with depolarization and repolarization, and local field potentials.

figure-24.alt: Handwritten outline notes for section 2, Neural activity is rhythmic: the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands, with a sketch of each wave.

figure-25.alt: Handwritten outline notes for section 3, Connection to slower body rhythms: activity in many brain areas syncs with breathing, and slow rhythms control the strength of faster ones.

figure-26.alt: Handwritten outline notes for section 4, Getting a signal from a recording: spike sorting steps, the Fourier transform, power spectrum and wavelet transform formulas, and open problems such as volume conduction.

figure-27.alt: Handwritten outline notes for section 5, Biological to artificial: the artificial neuron formula, the leaky integrate-and-fire model with a sketch of spiking, spiking neural networks and spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

figure-8.alt: Wavelet transform formula: W of a and b equals 1 over the square root of a, times the integral of x of t times the complex conjugate of psi of t minus b over a, d t.

figure-9.alt: Artificial neuron formula: y equals phi of the sum over i of w i times x i, plus b.

chapters.title: Predator-prey population dynamics
outline: The predator-prey cycle in the ecosystem

figure-1.alt: Line graph of hare and lynx populations from 1900 to 1935: both rise and fall in cycles of about 10 years, with lynx peaks following hare peaks.

figure-2.alt: Idealized graph of predator and prey populations over 25 years as two offset waves, the predator wave peaking just after the prey wave.

figure-3.alt: Pyramid of feeding levels: plants and other producers at the base, then herbivores, then carnivores, with top carnivores at the peak and soil decomposers beneath.

figure-4.alt: Bar graph of the mean number of aphids per ear and per shoot, before and after rain: there are fewer aphids after rain in both places.

figure-5.alt: Bar graph of hares per hectare from 1987 to 1994 under five treatments: control, added food, fertilizer, predator exclosure, and predator exclosure plus food; numbers peak around 1989 to 1991 and are highest with food added.
